warmup.q: A transfer debits A-1001 with one UpdateItem, then credits A-2002 with a second UpdateItem. The process is killed between the two calls. What does the table hold?
options: Neither change: DynamoDB rolls back the debit when the credit never arrives
The debit only: each UpdateItem commits on its own, and nothing ties the two together
Both changes: the SDK sends the credit again when the service restarts
Neither change, as long as both calls carried the same idempotency key
warmup.why: Each UpdateItem is atomic for its own item and nothing else. DynamoDB doesn't know the two calls belong together, so the debit stays and the credit never happens: 30.00 leaves one account and arrives nowhere. An idempotency key only stops a repeat; it doesn't undo a half-done sequence. Grouping writes so they happen together or not at all is what TransactWriteItems is for.

sections.h: One Query can return an account and its newest payments
sections.html:
Lesson 3's item collection held one account's payments. This lesson asks what a store with no joins does when a screen needs several kinds of record, and the answer is to store the join's result instead of computing it. The account screen in the payments app shows two things: the account's balance and its 20 newest payments. In Oracle that's one query with a join. DynamoDB has no joins. So build the screen up, one version at a time.

Version 1 copies the relational layout: an accounts table keyed by account id, and a payments table with partition key accountId and sort key createdAt. The screen is a GetItem on one table and a Query on the other. That's two requests where Oracle needed one, and it grows with every entity. The payment detail page wants the payment and its refunds, so that's a third table and a second pair of requests. The statement page wants the ledger, a fourth.

Version 2 puts every kind of item in one table. The key attributes get generic names, pk and sk, because they hold different things for different items. Give the account's own item, its payments, its refunds and its ledger entries the same partition key, ACCT#A-1001. Now they're one item collection, lesson 3's name for the items that share a partition key, stored together and sorted by sort key. Alex DeBrie calls this pre-joining: you store the result of the join instead of computing it on every read. Each item also carries a type attribute, so your code knows what came back.

Version 3 names the sort keys so that the order answers the question. DynamoDB compares sort keys byte by byte, so the collection reads LEDGER#..., then PAY#..., then the account item, then REFUND#.... In lesson 3's demo the account item was META, and M sorts before P. Read the collection backward to get the newest payments first, and you'd meet the account item last, after every payment. Rename it PROFILE. PA sorts before PR, so the profile now sits right after the newest payment. One Query, sk BETWEEN "PAY#" AND "PROFILE", read backward with Limit 21, returns the profile and then the 20 newest payments. The stepper shows it, and two more questions answered by the same collection.

A single table is a set of item collections whose sort keys you name on purpose, so that each screen is one contiguous run. That's the picture for this lesson. Indexes and transactions below add to it.

The cost is one request. A Query adds up the sizes of the items it reads and rounds up to the next 4 KB, so 21 items of about 300 bytes, about 6.3 KB, cost 2 read units with a strongly consistent read. DeBrie, who argues for this design, is plain about what it buys: the main win is fewer requests, and the savings from running fewer tables are marginal. The price is a table that looks, in his words, "more like machine code than a simple spreadsheet". You can't read it without the key design next to it.

sections.h: A global secondary index gives the same items a second address
sections.html:
The account collection can't answer two of the access patterns from lesson 2. AP2 asks for a payment by its id, and AP3 for a merchant's payments with one status in a time window. Neither question knows the account, so neither can name the partition. Lesson 2's answer was a second copy of the data under a different key. In DynamoDB that copy is a global secondary index (GSI).

You create a GSI by naming which attributes form its partition key and sort key. DynamoDB copies every item that has those attributes into the index, partitioned and sorted by them, and updates the copy after every write to the table. This table has two:

  • byPayment, partition key paymentId, sort key sk. Payments and refunds both carry paymentId, and PAY# sorts before REFUND#. So one Query for pay-81723 returns the payment, then its refunds in time order. That's AP2 and AP6 in one request.
  • byMerchant, partition key merchantId, sort key status then createdAt. AP3 fixes the merchant and the status with = and asks a range of createdAt.

That second index uses a feature DynamoDB added in November 2025: a GSI key can be built from up to four attributes for the partition key and four for the sort key. Before that, you glued FAILED#2026-11-07T09:40:27Z into one extra string attribute and kept it in step with status yourself. Lesson 2's no-gaps rule still holds, and DynamoDB enforces it. Ask for createdAt > 09:00 without status and the Query is refused (the demo below prints the error). One more snag: status is a DynamoDB reserved word, so the key condition must call it #status and map that name in expressionAttributeNames.

An item that lacks an index's key attributes isn't in that index. Profiles, ledger entries and claims have no merchantId, so byMerchant holds payments and nothing else. People call this a sparse index, and you can use it on purpose: give an attribute only to the items you want listed.

The copies aren't free, and they lag. A payment has the key attributes of both indexes, so one PutItem is three writes, each charged. DynamoDB updates a GSI asynchronously, so a payment written a moment ago can be missing from the merchant dashboard for a short time, and you can't ask a GSI for a strongly consistent read. DynamoDB answers "Consistent reads are not supported on global secondary indexes". Reads that must see every write, such as the balance check before a transfer, go to the table.

sections.h: TransactWriteItems: five writes that happen together or not at all
sections.html:
A transfer of 30.00 from A-1001 to A-2002 is five writes in this table. It debits A-1001's PROFILE, credits A-2002's PROFILE, puts a LEDGER# item into each account's collection, and claims the idempotency key, as lesson 3's payments did. The two accounts are different partitions, so they can sit on different machines. Build it up.

Version 1 sends five separate requests. Each one is atomic for its own item and for nothing else. Kill the process after the debit, and 30.00 has left A-1001 and arrived nowhere. A retry can't tell which of the five steps already ran.

Version 2 sends one BatchWriteItem. That saves round trips but promises nothing as a unit: the docs say some of a batch's writes can succeed while others fail. It also can't update an item or check a condition, only put and delete.

Version 3 is TransactWriteItems. DynamoDB applies every action in the request, or none of them. One request carries up to 100 actions on up to 100 distinct items, in one or more tables of the same account and Region, at most 4 MB in all. An action is a Put, an Update, a Delete or a ConditionCheck, and each can carry a condition. Here is the debit and the claim. The credit and the two ledger puts sit between them:

val debit = TransactWriteItem.builder().update(
    Update.builder().tableName(table)
        .key(Keys.key("ACCT#A-1001", "PROFILE"))
        .updateExpression("SET balanceMinor = balanceMinor - :amt")
        .conditionExpression("balanceMinor >= :amt")          // no overdraft
        .expressionAttributeValues(mapOf(":amt" to Keys.n(3_000)))
        .returnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure(ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure.ALL_OLD)
        .build()
).build()
val claim = TransactWriteItem.builder().put(
    Put.builder().tableName(table)
        .item(Keys.key("IDEMP#k-1", "IDEMP") + mapOf("transferId" to Keys.s("txf-k-1")))
        .conditionExpression("attribute_not_exists(pk)")      // first use of this key only
        .build()
).build()
ddb.transactWriteItems { it.transactItems(debit, credit, ledgerFrom, ledgerTo, claim) }

If any condition is false, nothing is written and the SDK throws TransactionCanceledException. Its cancellationReasons() has one entry per action, in the order you sent them. An action that was fine says None, and the one that failed says why, such as ConditionalCheckFailed. With ALL_OLD on an action, its reason also carries the item as it was. So the debit's reason tells you the balance you failed on, and an empty item means the account doesn't exist.

Two rules catch people. A transaction can't touch one item twice, so a transfer from A-1001 to A-1001 is refused as a whole. And the conditions are checked against the items as they are when the transaction runs, not against what your code read a moment earlier. That's the point: the check and the write are one step.

The same tool closes the gap lesson 3 left open. There, the claim and the payment were two writes, and a crash between them left a claim with no payment. The worked example below puts both into one transaction.

try.title: Watch a transfer commit, then fail as a whole
steps: Read TransferDemo.kt. transferActions builds the five actions; main sends three transfers: 30.00 with key k-1, 500.00 with key k-2, and k-1 again.
A-1001 starts with 100.00. Predict for each transfer: does it commit, which action's reason is not None, and what are the balances afterwards?

code.title: TransferDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.model.l04.demo import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.Put import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.TransactWriteItem import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.TransactionCanceledException import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.Update /** A transfer as one TransactWriteItems: it all happens, or none of it does. */ fun main() { val ddb = localClient() val table = "demo-single" createPaymentsTable(ddb, table) seedPayments(ddb, table) // A-1001 holds 100.00 EUR, A-2002 holds 50.00 EUR fun balances() = listOf("A-1001", "A-2002").joinToString(", ") { acct -> val item = ddb.getItem { it.tableName(table).key(mapOf("pk" to s("ACCT#$acct"), "sk" to s("PROFILE"))).consistentRead(true) }.item() "$acct ${item["balanceMinor"]!!.n()}" } fun ledgerCount() = ddb.query { it.tableName(table).keyConditionExpression("pk = :pk AND begins_with(sk, :l)") .expressionAttributeValues(mapOf(":pk" to s("ACCT#A-1001"), ":l" to s("LEDGER#"))).consistentRead(true) }.count() fun attempt(label: String, key: String, amount: Long) { try { ddb.transactWriteItems { it.transactItems(transferActions(table, key, "txf-$key", "A-1001", "A-2002", amount)) } println("$label: committed") } catch (e: TransactionCanceledException) { println("$label: ${e.javaClass.simpleName}") // one reason per action, in the order they were sent val names = listOf("debit A-1001", "credit A-2002", "ledger A-1001", "ledger A-2002", "claim") e.cancellationReasons().forEachIndexed { i, r -> println(" [$i] %-14s %s".format(names[i], r.code())) } } println(" balances: ${balances()}; A-1001 ledger entries: ${ledgerCount()}") } println("before: ${balances()}; A-1001 ledger entries: ${ledgerCount()}") attempt("transfer 30.00 with key k-1", "k-1", 3_000) attempt("transfer 500.00 with key k-2", "k-2", 50_000) attempt("retry of k-1", "k-1", 3_000) ddb.close() } /** Debit, credit, two ledger entries and the idempotency claim: five actions, one request. */ fun transferActions(table: String, key: String, transferId: String, from: String, to: String, amount: Long): List<TransactWriteItem> { val amt = mapOf(":amt" to n(amount)) fun ledger(account: String, signed: Long) = TransactWriteItem.builder().put(Put.builder().tableName(table).item(mapOf( "pk" to s("ACCT#$account"), "sk" to s("LEDGER#2026-11-07T12:30:00.000Z#$transferId"), "type" to s("LEDGER"), "transferId" to s(transferId), "amountMinor" to n(signed), )).build()).build() return listOf( TransactWriteItem.builder().update(Update.builder().tableName(table) .key(mapOf("pk" to s("ACCT#$from"), "sk" to s("PROFILE"))) .updateExpression("SET balanceMinor = balanceMinor - :amt") .conditionExpression("balanceMinor >= :amt") // no overdraft .expressionAttributeValues(amt).build()).build(), TransactWriteItem.builder().update(Update.builder().tableName(table) .key(mapOf("pk" to s("ACCT#$to"), "sk" to s("PROFILE"))) .updateExpression("SET balanceMinor = balanceMinor + :amt") .conditionExpression("attribute_exists(pk)") // the target account must exist .expressionAttributeValues(amt).build()).build(), ledger(from, -amount), ledger(to, amount), TransactWriteItem.builder().put(Put.builder().tableName(table) .item(mapOf("pk" to s("IDEMP#$key"), "sk" to s("IDEMP"), "type" to s("CLAIM"), "transferId" to s(transferId))) .conditionExpression("attribute_not_exists(pk)") // first use of this key only .build()).build(), ) }

before: A-1001 10000, A-2002 5000; A-1001 ledger entries: 2
transfer 30.00 with key k-1: committed
  balances: A-1001 7000, A-2002 8000; A-1001 ledger entries: 3
transfer 500.00 with key k-2: TransactionCanceledException
  [0] debit A-1001   ConditionalCheckFailed
  [1] credit A-2002  None
  [2] ledger A-1001  None
  [3] ledger A-2002  None
  [4] claim          None
  balances: A-1001 7000, A-2002 8000; A-1001 ledger entries: 3
retry of k-1: TransactionCanceledException
  [0] debit A-1001   None
  [1] credit A-2002  None
  [2] ledger A-1001  None
  [3] ledger A-2002  None

The first transfer writes all five items. The second fails only the debit's condition, and yet the credit, both ledger entries and the claim are missing too: nothing was written. The retry of k-1 would have had the money (70.00 left), but its claim already exists, so the whole transaction is cancelled and nothing moves twice. Reasons come back in the order the actions were sent, which is how your code tells these cases apart.

refs.title: Amazon DynamoDB Transactions: how it works

sections.h: What a transaction costs, and what it doesn't promise
sections.html:
A transaction costs twice what the same writes cost alone. DynamoDB does two underlying writes for every item in it, one to prepare and one to commit. The five-item transfer, every item under 1 KB, uses 10 write units instead of 5. It still uses them when it's cancelled. DynamoDB Local doesn't model this in the ConsumedCapacity it reports, so take the number from the AWS docs, not from the demo.

Transactions also collide. If two transactions touch the same item at the same time, DynamoDB cancels one with the reason TransactionConflict. The AWS SDK doesn't retry a cancelled transaction, so your code has to. A hot account that many transfers touch at once will see conflicts, which is one more reason to keep transactions small. The AWS docs say the same: don't group writes into a transaction unless correctness needs it.

Know what a transaction doesn't promise. Its isolation is serializable against single-item calls (GetItem, PutItem, UpdateItem, DeleteItem) and against other transactions. Against Query, Scan and BatchGetItem it's read-committed. You never see a write from a transaction that failed, but a Query running during a transfer can see some of the transfer's items in their new state and others in their old one. To read both accounts as one snapshot, use TransactGetItems. Indexes and DynamoDB Streams receive a transaction's changes gradually, so a stream consumer can't assume the five writes arrive together. With global tables, the guarantees hold only in the Region where you made the call.

Retries need two guards, at two different levels. The first is the client request token. Send the same TransactWriteItems with the same ClientRequestToken within 10 minutes and DynamoDB returns success without writing anything again. Change any parameter under the same token and it throws IdempotentParameterMismatchException. When you don't set a token, the AWS SDK fills in a fresh UUID on every call (a request interceptor shows it), which covers the SDK's own retries of that call. The second guard is the claim item. A retry your code builds itself, say a Kafka redelivery an hour later with a new ledger timestamp, is a new request with a new token. Only the claim's condition stops that one, for as long as the claim lives.

Single-table design isn't always the right call. DeBrie names two cases where he wouldn't use it: a new application whose questions aren't known yet, and GraphQL, where each resolver makes its own call anyway (lesson 9 shows why). Add a third from your own world: a back-office tool whose questions change every sprint. For the payments core, with its six access patterns written down and stable, use it.

Under the API, DynamoDB is a fleet of request routers and storage nodes. The Partitioning track's lesson on DynamoDB under the hood goes underneath: how a table is cut into partitions, how each partition is copied to three availability zones, why a partition splits, and how to choose and set up capacity.

try.title: Send one transaction twice with the same token
steps: Read ClientTokenDemo.kt. It sends one transfer three times with the same ClientRequestToken: as is, as is again, then with 40.00 instead of 30.00. The idempotency claim is in the request too, but look at what the second call returns.
Predict A-1001's balance after the second call, and what the third call does.
Run it. Then stop DynamoDB Local: docker compose -f env/dynamodb.yml down -v.

code.title: ClientTokenDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.model.l04.demo import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.IdempotentParameterMismatchException import java.util.UUID /** The request-level guard: a ClientRequestToken makes a repeated TransactWriteItems a no-op for 10 minutes. */ fun main() { val ddb = localClient() val table = "demo-single" createPaymentsTable(ddb, table) seedPayments(ddb, table) // A-1001 holds 100.00 EUR, A-2002 holds 50.00 EUR fun balance() = ddb.getItem { it.tableName(table).key(mapOf("pk" to s("ACCT#A-1001"), "sk" to s("PROFILE"))).consistentRead(true) }.item()["balanceMinor"]!!.n() // at most 36 characters; a fresh one per run, because DynamoDB remembers a token // for 10 minutes after the request that used it finishes val token = UUID.randomUUID().toString() fun send(key: String, amount: Long) = ddb.transactWriteItems { it.transactItems(transferActions(table, key, "txf-$key", "A-1001", "A-2002", amount)) .clientRequestToken(token) } send("k-7", 3_000) println("first call with the token: A-1001 = ${balance()}") send("k-7", 3_000) // say the response was lost and the caller sends the identical request again println("same request, same token again: A-1001 = ${balance()} (success, nothing written)") try { send("k-7", 4_000) } catch (e: IdempotentParameterMismatchException) { println("same token, amount 40.00: ${e.javaClass.simpleName}") } ddb.close() }

try.expect:
first call with the token:        A-1001 = 7000
same request, same token again:   A-1001 = 7000  (success, nothing written)
same token, amount 40.00:         IdempotentParameterMismatchException

The second call returns success, not a cancelled transaction: DynamoDB recognises the token and replies as it did the first time, without writing. That's what a caller whose response got lost needs. Change the request under the same token and DynamoDB refuses it outright. The token is remembered for 10 minutes after the request finishes, which is why the demo makes a fresh one per run; a retry that comes later, or arrives as a new request, is caught by the claim instead.

analogy: A single table works like a filing cabinet where every customer gets one drawer. Inside the drawer, the dividers are labelled so that the things you pull out together sit next to each other: the customer's profile card right behind the newest receipts, the bank statements at the front, the refund slips at the back. Pulling the account screen is one grab from one spot. A global secondary index is a second cabinet, kept by a clerk who photocopies every receipt into a drawer per merchant. A transaction is a notary who won't stamp any of five documents until all five are in order, and stamps none if one is wrong. The analogy breaks in two places: the clerk with the photocopier is always a little behind, so the merchant cabinet can miss the newest receipt, and the notary charges twice for every document, even when the stamping is called off.
world: Your Oracle transfer is probably a @Transactional method in Quarkus: two UPDATEs and two INSERTs, then COMMIT, with WHERE balance_minor >= :amt guarding the debit. That design moves to DynamoDB as one TransactWriteItems, with the WHERE clause turned into a condition expression. It earns its place in a wallet or prepaid-balance service fed by a Kafka topic of transfer commands. Use the command's own id as the idempotency key, so a consumer that gets the message again after a rebalance hits ConditionalCheckFailed on the claim instead of moving money twice. In Temporal, put the TransactWriteItems in an activity. The SDK's token covers its own quick retries of the call; the claim covers the activity retry that comes an hour later with a fresh request.
mistake: The most common mistake is reading the balance with GetItem, checking it in Kotlin, and then writing the new balance: if (balance >= amount) put(balance - amount), sometimes even inside TransactWriteItems. Two transfers that run at the same moment both read 100.00, both pass the check, and both write 70.00. One debit is lost, or the account goes negative. People do it because it's how the code reads in their head, and a transaction around it feels safe. It isn't, because the read happened outside the transaction. The fix: put the check in a condition (balanceMinor >= :amt) and the arithmetic in the update expression (SET balanceMinor = balanceMinor - :amt), so DynamoDB checks and changes the item in one step.

compare.title: The same transfer in Oracle and in DynamoDB

a.label: Oracle
a.title: one database transaction
a.html: -- row locks are taken as you go; the session decides when to commit UPDATE account SET balance_minor = balance_minor - 3000 WHERE account_id = 'A-1001' AND balance_minor >= 3000; -- 0 rows updated? the application sees it and calls ROLLBACK UPDATE account SET balance_minor = balance_minor + 3000 WHERE account_id = 'A-2002'; INSERT INTO ledger_entry (account_id, transfer_id, amount_minor) VALUES ('A-1001', 'txf-k-1', -3000); INSERT INTO ledger_entry (account_id, transfer_id, amount_minor) VALUES ('A-2002', 'txf-k-1', 3000); INSERT INTO idempotency_key (idem_key, transfer_id) VALUES ('k-1', 'txf-k-1'); COMMIT;

b.label: DynamoDB
b.title: one TransactWriteItems request
b.html: // every action is known before the request is sent; no reads in between ddb.transactWriteItems { it.transactItems( debit, // Update A-1001 PROFILE, condition balanceMinor >= :amt credit, // Update A-2002 PROFILE, condition attribute_exists(pk) ledgerFrom, // Put LEDGER#...#txf-k-1 into A-1001's collection ledgerTo, // Put LEDGER#...#txf-k-1 into A-2002's collection claim, // Put IDEMP#k-1, condition attribute_not_exists(pk) ) } // any false condition: TransactionCanceledException, nothing written

compare.note: Both are all or nothing. Oracle runs a conversation: the session takes locks statement by statement, can read and decide halfway, and commits when it says so. DynamoDB takes the whole transaction in one request. There are no reads in the middle, only conditions that it checks for you, and at most 100 items. Oracle's unique constraint on idem_key plays the role of attribute_not_exists, and the AND balance_minor >= 3000 guard becomes a condition expression. DynamoDB charges two writes per item for the privilege; Oracle charges in redo, locks and a primary that has to take every write.

worked.title: Close lesson 3's gap: the claim and the payment in one transaction

steps.say: In lesson 3, createPayment made two calls: the conditional put of the claim, then the plain put of the payment. A crash between them leaves a claim with no payment, and every retry is then answered with a payment that doesn't exist.
steps.code: claims.putItem(claimRequest) // 1. conditional: the key is ours // a crash here: the claim exists, the payment never will payments.putItem(toItem(cmd)) // 2. the payment

steps.say: Build both writes as actions. The claim keeps lesson 3's condition and asks for ALL_OLD, so a failed claim comes back with the winner's item. Its payment id goes in an attribute called forPayment: an attribute named paymentId would put the claim into the byPayment index next to the payment.
steps.code: val now = cmd.at.epochSecond val claim = TransactWriteItem.builder().put( Put.builder().tableName(table) .item(Keys.key(Keys.claim(cmd.idempotencyKey), Keys.CLAIM) + mapOf( "type" to Keys.s("CLAIM"), "forPayment" to Keys.s(cmd.paymentId), "fingerprint" to Keys.s(cmd.fingerprint()), "expiresAt" to Keys.n(now + 86_400))) .conditionExpression("attribute_not_exists(pk) OR expiresAt < :now") .expressionAttributeValues(mapOf(":now" to Keys.n(now))) .returnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure(ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure.ALL_OLD) .build() ).build() val payment = TransactWriteItem.builder().put( Put.builder().tableName(table).item(Keys.paymentItem( Payment(cmd.paymentId, cmd.accountId, cmd.merchantId, cmd.amountMinor, cmd.currency, "AUTHORIZED", cmd.at) )).build() ).build()

steps.say: Send them together. If the claim's condition fails, the payment isn't written either, and the reason at index 0 carries the live claim. Compare fingerprints as before. Any other reason, such as TransactionConflict, goes back to the caller to retry with the same key.
steps.code: return try { ddb.transactWriteItems { it.transactItems(claim, payment) } CreateResult.Created(cmd.paymentId) } catch (e: TransactionCanceledException) { val reason = e.cancellationReasons()[0] if (reason.code() != "ConditionalCheckFailed") throw e // a conflict: retry later val live = reason.item() // the claim that won, via ALL_OLD val first = live.getValue("forPayment").s() if (live.getValue("fingerprint").s() == cmd.fingerprint()) CreateResult.Replayed(first) else CreateResult.Mismatch(first) }

steps.say: Check what changed. The crash window is gone, and the extra read after a failed claim is gone too. The bill is higher: two items in a transaction cost two writes each.
steps.code:
two puts (lesson 3)        one transaction
requests on success      2                          1
write units, table       2                          4
crash between writes     claim without payment      impossible
duplicate request        put fails, then GetItem    cancelled, claim in the reason

drill.title: The debit action from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson and the lab. Write the TransactWriteItem that debits 30.00 from A-1001's PROFILE item, only if the balance covers it, and returns the old item when the condition fails. Use the low-level client's builders. Then say in one sentence why the check must live in the condition rather than in Kotlin.

answer.html: val debit = TransactWriteItem.builder().update( Update.builder().tableName("payments") .key(mapOf("pk" to AttributeValue.fromS("ACCT#A-1001"), "sk" to AttributeValue.fromS("PROFILE"))) .updateExpression("SET balanceMinor = balanceMinor - :amt") // the arithmetic happens on the server .conditionExpression("balanceMinor >= :amt") // checked against the item as it is now .expressionAttributeValues(mapOf(":amt" to AttributeValue.fromN("3000"))) .returnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure(ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure.ALL_OLD) .build() ).build() // A balance read in Kotlin can be stale by the time the write lands; the condition is checked // in the same step as the update, so two concurrent debits can't both pass it.

recap: Single-table design puts several item types under one partition key and names their sort keys so that each screen is one contiguous run. PROFILE sorts right after PAY#, so one backward Query returns the account and its newest payments.

A global secondary index stores a second copy of every item that has its key attributes, under its own partition and sort key. Each copy costs a write, it lags the table, and it can't be read strongly consistently.
Since November 2025 a GSI key can have up to four partition and four sort attributes, so you don't glue status#createdAt by hand. The sort attributes still go left to right, with no gaps.
TransactWriteItems applies up to 100 actions on distinct items all or nothing. One false condition cancels everything, and cancellationReasons() says which action failed, in request order.

A transaction costs two writes per item, cancelled or not. Put checks in conditions and arithmetic in update expressions. A client token stops a repeated request for 10 minutes; a claim item stops any retry that uses the same key.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why the payments service keeps accounts, payments, refunds and ledger entries in one DynamoDB table instead of four, and whether a transfer could just be two UpdateItems. Explain both.
explain.answer: DynamoDB has no joins, so every table you read is another request. In one table, an account's items share one partition key and sit together, sorted by sort key, and the key names are chosen so that each screen is one contiguous run. The account item is called PROFILE so it sorts right after the payments, which means one backward Query returns the account and its 20 newest payments. Questions that don't know the account, like a payment by id or a merchant's failed payments, get a global secondary index: a second copy of the same items under another key, which costs extra writes and lags slightly. The price is a table you can't read without the key design next to it. As for the transfer: two UpdateItems are two separate atomic writes, so a crash between them loses money. One TransactWriteItems puts the debit with its balance condition, the credit, both ledger entries and the idempotency claim into one request that DynamoDB applies completely or not at all, and it tells us which condition failed. It costs two writes per item, so we keep transactions to the writes that have to happen together.

deeper.html:
Before multi-attribute keys, single-table designs often used index overloading. Every item got two generic attributes, gsi1pk and gsi1sk, and each item type filled them with something different: a payment put MERCH#M-0042 and FAILED#2026-11-07T09:40:27Z there, a refund put its payment id there, and so on. One index then served several access patterns, at the cost of a key design that only a table of item types can explain. You'll meet it in older codebases and in DeBrie's writing. With up to four attributes per key half since November 2025, you can often name the real attributes instead. Each GSI still costs its own write on every item it holds, so overloading one index can still be cheaper than three separate ones.

TransactGetItems is the read side: up to 100 Get actions that DynamoDB returns as one consistent snapshot. Use it for a statement that must show both sides of a transfer in the same state. A Query of one collection is read-committed against transactions, so it could see the debit's new balance next to a ledger page from before.

With provisioned capacity, a transaction that hits a busy item can still be throttled or conflict, and the right retry is the same request with the same idempotency key, after a short random backoff. Because the AWS SDK fills a fresh client token into every call it makes, a retry that you code yourself is a new request to DynamoDB; the claim item is what makes it safe.

DynamoDB Streams, the table's change log, records a transaction's item changes as separate records, possibly interleaved with other writes. A consumer that rebuilds balances from the stream should group by transferId, not assume the five records arrive together.
